reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: The phenotype spans central and peripheral nervous system involvement, from limbic encephalitis to peripheral nerve hyperexcitability
Peripheral hyperexcitability manifests as neuromyotonia — muscle twitching, cramps, stiffness, and myokymia — often with neuropathic pain
Morvan syndrome combines neuromyotonia, dysautonomia, severe insomnia (agrypnia excitata), and fluctuating encephalopathy
Antibodies target contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2), a component of the former voltage-gated potassium channel complex
Weight loss, dysautonomia, and neuropathic pain are frequent accompanying features
CASPR2 disease carries a stronger association with thymoma than LGI1 disease, so mediastinal imaging is important

Treatment follows autoimmune encephalitis principles with first-line corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, and rituximab for refractory cases, alongside tumour removal where present
reference.pathophysiology: Antibodies bind contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2), a cell-adhesion protein clustered at the juxtaparanodal region of myelinated axons and within the hippocampus, where it organises voltage-gated potassium channels. Loss of CASPR2 function reduces potassium-channel clustering and raises axonal and neuronal excitability, generating peripheral neuromyotonia and, centrally, limbic hyperexcitability and encephalopathy. The combined central and peripheral distribution of the antigen explains the wide clinical spectrum, and in a subset the immune response is driven by an underlying thymoma.
additionalDifferentials: LGI1 and other surface-antigen limbic encephalitides
Isaacs syndrome (acquired neuromyotonia) of other cause
Fatal familial or other causes of severe insomnia
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid testing for CASPR2 antibodies
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography for neuromyotonic and myokymic discharges
MRI of the brain to assess for limbic involvement
Mediastinal CT to screen for thymoma
Autonomic function assessment where dysautonomia is prominent
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis to exclude infection and assess inflammation
redFlags: Intractable insomnia and fluctuating encephalopathy of Morvan syndrome
Rapidly progressive cognitive decline or seizures
Identification of a thymoma requiring surgical management
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond well to immunotherapy and tumour treatment, though recovery of neuropathic pain and dysautonomia can lag. Morvan syndrome and thymoma-associated disease may follow a more severe or relapsing course.
pitfalls: Attributing neuromyotonia to a primary muscle disorder and missing the autoimmune basis
Interpreting insomnia and behavioural change as psychiatric rather than encephalopathic
Assuming central and peripheral features cannot coexist in one disorder
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin and/or plasma exchange
Escalation to second-line immunosuppression such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide in refractory disease
Screening for and resection of an underlying thymoma
Symptomatic control of peripheral nerve hyperexcitability and neuropathic pain with membrane-stabilising agents such as carbamazepine or gabapentinoids
Management of dysautonomia and severe insomnia, particularly in Morvan syndrome
Monitoring for relapse with clinical review and antibody testing
Multidisciplinary neurology, neuroimmunology and, where thymoma is present, thoracic surgery input
